Myanmar genocide ruling is a watershed moment in international justice – with huge ramifications for other cases
items.summary: The International Court of Justice’s historic ruling of genocide against Myanmar on Nov. 19, 2026, will have significant consequences for the parties involved in the case – and potentially some who are not. The Hague’s highly anticipated judgment in Gambia v. Myanmar is a major victory for Gambia, the tiny west African nation that filed a complaint with the court against Myanmar in 2019. It is also a major moment of accountability for the military leadership of Myanmar. But as an expert in genocide and mass atrocity prevention, I believe the ruling goes far beyond these nations. Indeed, it is also a watershed moment for international legal justice that is bound to have important effects on the court’s other ongoing genocide cases, particularly the case of South Africa v. Israel . Rohingya refugees watch the International Court of Justice ruling on a screen at a camp in Bangladesh’s Cox’s Bazar on Nov. items.title: Rohingya in Bangladesh welcome UN court's genocide verdict but say they want to go home to Myanmar
items.summary: By Shamimul Islam Faisal COX’S BAZAR, Bangladesh (AP) — Hundreds of Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh sat in front of a big screen at their sprawling camp in Cox’s Bazar, watching the news from the Netherlands, where the U.N.'s top court ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya minority in a brutal 2017 military operation. For many, the historic verdict on Thursday represented a “small victory” — offering a glimmer of hope that someday they would be able to return safely to their homes in Myanmar, across the border from Bangladesh . Only then, some said, will they be “fully satisfied.” It was a landmark judgment, finding Myanmar responsible for the crime against the country’s ethnic Rohingya — the first time the court ruled that a state committed genocide. The Hague-based International Court of Justice also ordered Myanmar’s military-supported government to allow the Rohingya to return home safely, pay reparations to the Rohingya Muslims and prosecute those suspected of having committed genocide. items.title: You have a good case: Supreme Court issues notice on bail petition despite POCSO accused wanting to withdraw case
items.summary: In an unusual turn of events, Supreme Court on Monday refused to allow a lawyer to withdraw a bail petition filed on behalf of an accused booked under the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act (POCSO Act). The Court instead chose to seek the State's response after noting that the underlying relationship between the accused and victim appeared to be consensual. The order issuing notice was passed by Justices JB Pardiwala and Vinod K Chandran when the petitioner's counsel sought to pull out of the proceedings. As soon as the matter was called, the advocate informed the Bench that she had instructions from her client to withdraw the petition with liberty to approach the trial court for bail. Taken aback by the request, Justice Pardiwala asked why the petitioner was backing out when she appeared to have a strong case on merits. "Why are you withdrawing?" Justice Pardiwala asked. "With liberty to approach the trial court for bail," the counsel replied. "Why? You don't have a good case? You are praying for bail? Who has instructed you to withdraw?" the judge pressed further. items.title: Punjab & Haryana High Court denies anticipatory bail to man accused of stealing his own vehicle from police station
items.summary: The Punjab and Haryana High Court recently denied anticipatory bail to a man accused of stealing his own vehicle from a police station in Hisar last month [ Dharmender Dudi alias Dharmender alias Mahender Dharamender Dudi v State of Haryana ]. The vehicle had been impounded after the driver was allegedly found driving while intoxicated. Justice Vikram Aggarwal declined to consider the driver's claim that his vehicle was taken away by the police as he did not succumb to their monetary demands. The judge said the accused had committed a serious offence by allegedly stealing the impounded car from the premises of the police station. "It indeed is a very serious offence where the petitioner dared to commit a theft in the police station. This Court is not inclined to go into the version of the petitioner at this stage that he was intentionally issued challans and that his vehicle was taken away since he did not succumb to monetary demands. These allegations do not outweigh the allegations in the FIR," the Court said. This situation needs to be corrected. The petitioner deserves to be released from custody,” the Court said. items.title: Allahabad High Court sends man to jail for recording hearing, bars litigants from carrying phones into court
items.summary: The Allahabad High Court recently ordered the arrest of a man who was found recording court proceedings on his mobile phone and prohibited litigants from carrying mobile phones into courtrooms [Kuldeep Batra v State of UP and Another]. The Court also passed directions prohibiting litigants from carrying mobile phones inside courtrooms. On November 19, Justice Vikram D Chauhan found Raj Kulshrestha, a resident of Varanasi, recording the proceedings taking place in his courtroom. Kulshrestha, who was in possession of an entry pass for the advocates’ chamber and not the courtroom, could not explain the reason for recording the proceedings. The Court staff, who seized his phone, found at least three videos of court proceedings there. The Court then ordered Kulshrestha be taken into custody and produced again on November 20 at 10 am. He was directed to be produced before the Chief Judicial Magistrate, Prayagraj and granted a liberty to seek bail.
